newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Mexicans not so impressed by debt payments.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mexicans not so impressed by debt payments.

text.p: As foreign investors feted Mexico for its unexpected early repayment of $5 billion to the United States and the IMF, Mexican analysts on Thursday wondered how much of the good cheer was just hype.

Mexicans, who endured the debt crisis of the 1980s, are deeply cynical about foreign borrowing and it was not long before even the most untrained observers saw the payment meant no drop in Mexico's $100 billion total foreign debt.

To repay the oil-backed emergency loans, extended by President Bill Clinton in February 1995 when Mexico was on the brink of financial collapse, Mexico mostly used money it had borrowed at longer maturities in the global bond markets.
"Its borrowing from Peter to pay Paul," acknowledged Mexico's ambassador to Washington Jesus Silva Herzog, even though he stressed price conditions were now better.

Sergio Sarmiento, head of news at broadcaster TV Azteca, wrote in a newspaper column that the $100 million the government says it will save from lower interest rates was the equivalent of just five days normal debt servicing.
"From an economic point of view, the transaction is not that important," he wrote.

He said the early payment was mostly politically driven ahead of hotly-contested mid-term congressional elections in July and was aimed at erasing a loan that was an unpopular stigma of crisis among Mexicans.

Nevertheless, Mexico's stock market surged on Wednesday's news. Brokers said the repayment would help Mexico's image abroad and attract more foreign cash. The bolsa continued to break record ground on Thursday, rising 0.62 percent mid-morning to 3,750.96 points, before profit-taking set in.
In major financial centers, players touted the early payment, three years ahead of schedule, as a sign Mexico would be able to access cheaper credit and may even have its debt rating upgraded soon.

New York rating agencies, however, said no Mexico rating changes were in the pipeline. Also, Mexico has been obtaining steadily-improving access to bond markets for more than a year now, as memories of its December 1994 crisis faded.

On the local stock market, a buying spree has been underway since the New Year, with investors seeking to make quick profits from a growing economy and sliding interest rates, before mid-term elections in July cloud the horizon.
Analysts said there was a sense players had seized on the pre-payment news to fan their profits, even though it had little impact on Mexico's economic outlook.
"It's a bit artificial this euphoria," said Roberto Blum, analyst at the Center for Development Investigations.
"When (investors) see corporate results in March, they are going to immediately realize that this rally does not respond to the economic situation, it is a result of falling interest rates."
Ordinary Mexicans, still suffering from a recession in 1995 that was the worst in 50 years, were not likely to be impressed by the news, he added.
"People still feel sceptical," he said. "Though the economy is growing, they are not seeing the improvement at the micro level, in terms of companies and jobs."

Alberto Barranco Chavarria, a business columnist for Reforma newspaper, painted the pre-payment as a "merry-go-round of hype" that caused no jubilation on the streets of Mexico, however much it cheered the Bolsa.

He noted that $550 million of the pre-payment came from debts owed to the government by state oil firm Petroleos Mexicanos -- money, he said, that could have been better spent meeting urgent social needs.
Analysts pointed out that Mexico also still owes some $10.5 billion to the International Monetary Fund, money that it is paying back far slower than it repaid the U.S. Treasury.
((-- Mexico City newsroom +525 728-9560))
